title: Consolation and desolation
hookLine: moods that draw you toward or away from God

cards: Here's a question for any ordinary afternoon: which way am I drifting? Not how am I doing. Which way.
Back on day one hundred six, a dry prayer still counted. Ignatius goes further, with rules for noticing movements inside a person.
His account traces them to the sickbed from a week ago: the shattered leg, the reading, the daydreams. Some daydreams left him dry and restless. Others left him content and drawn toward God.
So he watched the aftertaste. His name for the second pull is today's word: consolation.

teach.b: Consolation, for Ignatius, is any movement inside that draws a person toward God: being set on fire with love of God, tears that move toward love, any growth in faith, hope and love, an inner joy and quiet that pulls toward heavenly things.
Desolation is the opposite pull: darkness, restlessness, a tug toward low things, feeling without hope or love, lazy, lukewarm, sad, as if cut off from God. Here's the surprise.
Consolation isn't the same as feeling good, and desolation isn't the same as feeling bad. Ignatius counts tears of grief over one's sins as consolation, because they draw toward God.
And a cheerful, busy week can be desolation underneath, if it's quietly drifting away.
The test is direction, not temperature.

Paul's list works like a compass: "But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith." When those grow, something's moving the right way. Ignatius adds a subtler detail.
The same feeling can mean different things depending on where a person is heading. For someone sliding toward harm, a nagging unease can be a mercy, a knock on the door.
For someone trying to grow toward God, a voice saying what's the point can be the pull away. So he asks people to notice the arrow under the mood.

And desolation isn't automatically a verdict. Ignatius gives three reasons it comes: sometimes our own slackness, sometimes a testing, sometimes to show that consolation is a gift, not an achievement.
It's weather to read, not a sentence passed. And if what's the point ever turns into thoughts of ending your life, please reach out: call or text 988 in the US, or local emergency help.

how: In Ignatian spirituality, people notice consolation and desolation in the daily examen and talk them over with a spiritual director, who helps them read which way the movements are pulling.

o: a small prize given to someone who didn't win the race
a cheerful mood that proves a person is close to God
Ignatius' word for any inner pull toward God, even through tears

games.q: the two pulls — tap the pairs.
p: a pull away, dark and restless

s: Ignatius counts tears of grief over one's sins as consolation, because they draw toward God.
for Ignatius, desolation includes feeling as if cut off from God
darkness, restlessness, without hope or love, as if cut off from God.
in Ignatius' rules, desolation always means you've done something wrong
sometimes it's our own slackness, he says, but it can also be a testing, or a lesson that consolation is a gift.

games.q: a cheerful, busy week, but you've quietly stopped caring about anyone outside your own plans. by Ignatius' test, what is it?
o: possibly desolation: the arrow points away.
games.why: the test is direction, not temperature. a happy surface can sit on top of a drift away.

practice: Run back over the day like a short film, watching for direction, not good or bad moments.
Where did something open you up, toward people, toward God, if that's your language, and where did something close you down or make everything feel pointless?
Name one of each, and if you pray, thank God for the first and bring him the second.

wordCard.voice: Consolation. Ignatius' word for any movement inside that draws a person toward God, and toward faith, hope and love, even when it comes with tears.

orig.note: Latin: comfort, solace, the word behind the English consolation.

carryVoice: Your line: which way am I drifting? The arrow matters more than the mood. See you tomorrow.
